prompt: What is inflation?

options.label: A
options.text: A sustained increase in the price level

options.label: B
options.text: A rise in the price of one product only

options.label: C
options.text: A sustained fall in the price level

options.label: D
options.text: A fall in the rate at which the price level rises

explanation: Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level. A single price increase is not sufficient because inflation concerns the average level of prices across the economy.
reference: 4.6 Price stability | 4.6.1 definition of inflation, deflation and disinflation | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: What is deflation?

options.label: A
options.text: A fall in inflation while prices still rise

options.label: B
options.text: A sustained fall in the price level

options.label: C
options.text: A fall in the price of one product only

options.label: D
options.text: A sustained rise in the price level

explanation: Deflation is a sustained decrease in the general price level, so the inflation rate is negative.
reference: 4.6 Price stability | 4.6.1 definition of inflation, deflation and disinflation | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: What is disinflation?

options.label: A
options.text: A sustained fall in the price level

options.label: B
options.text: A fall in the inflation rate while the price level is still rising

options.label: C
options.text: A rise in the inflation rate from one positive rate to a higher one

options.label: D
options.text: An unchanged general price level for every individual product

explanation: Disinflation means inflation is slowing. The inflation rate falls but remains positive, so the general price level continues to rise more slowly.
reference: 4.6 Price stability | 4.6.1 definition of inflation, deflation and disinflation | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: The inflation rate falls from 7% to 3%. What has occurred?

options.label: A
options.text: Deflation

options.label: B
options.text: Hyperinflation

options.label: C
options.text: Price-level stability with no price changes

options.label: D
options.text: Disinflation

explanation: The inflation rate remains positive, so prices are still rising on average. Because the rate has fallen, the economy is experiencing disinflation.
reference: 4.6 Price stability | 4.6.1 definition of inflation, deflation and disinflation | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: The inflation rate is -2%. What does this indicate?

options.label: A
options.text: Disinflation

options.label: B
options.text: Deflation

options.label: C
options.text: Demand-pull inflation only

options.label: D
options.text: Unchanged prices

explanation: A negative inflation rate means the general price level is falling, which is deflation.
reference: 4.6 Price stability | 4.6.1 definition of inflation, deflation and disinflation | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: Which statement is correct when the inflation rate falls from 5% to 2%?

options.label: A
options.text: Prices fall 3%

options.label: B
options.text: The price level returns to its earlier level

options.label: C
options.text: Every individual product price rises exactly 2% over the period

options.label: D
options.text: Prices still rise, but more slowly

explanation: A positive 2% inflation rate means the general price level is still rising. The decrease from 5% to 2% is disinflation, not deflation.
reference: 4.6 Price stability | 4.6.1 definition of inflation, deflation and disinflation | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Which statement about inflation is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Every price must rise by the same percentage

options.label: B
options.text: The prices of all goods must rise while all services prices remain unchanged

options.label: C
options.text: Not every individual price has to rise for the price level to rise

options.label: D
options.text: Inflation can occur only when the price of imported goods rises

explanation: Inflation measures the average change in the general price level. Some prices may fall or remain unchanged while the weighted average rises.
reference: 4.6 Price stability | 4.6.1 definition of inflation, deflation and disinflation | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: What does the Consumer Price Index (CPI) measure?

options.label: A
options.text: The value of domestic output

options.label: B
options.text: The average wage received by all employed workers

options.label: C
options.text: Price changes for a representative consumer basket

options.label: D
options.text: Households’ money holdings

explanation: The CPI is a weighted index of the prices of a representative basket of consumer goods and services purchased by households.
reference: 4.6 Price stability | 4.6.2 measurement of changes in the price level: consumer price index (CPI) and possible difficulties in measurement | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: Why are weights used in a CPI?

options.label: A
options.text: To reflect expenditure shares

options.label: B
options.text: To give each product an equal contribution to the index

options.label: C
options.text: To remove quality changes

options.label: D
options.text: To ensure that the index represents every household’s expenditure pattern equally

explanation: Weights reflect the relative importance of items in household expenditure. A price change in a heavily purchased category therefore has more influence on the CPI.
reference: 4.6 Price stability | 4.6.2 measurement of changes in the price level: consumer price index (CPI) and possible difficulties in measurement | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: In a CPI, what value is normally assigned to the base year?

options.label: C
options.text: The inflation rate in that year

explanation: Price indices commonly set the base-year index equal to 100. Later index values are interpreted relative to that base.
reference: 4.6 Price stability | 4.6.2 measurement of changes in the price level: consumer price index (CPI) and possible difficulties in measurement | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: Why is a household spending survey used when constructing a CPI?

options.label: A
options.text: To estimate unemployment

options.label: B
options.text: To determine the maximum output attainable with available resources

options.label: C
options.text: To measure firms’ profits

options.label: D
options.text: To set weights using expenditure shares

explanation: A household spending survey shows how much consumers spend on different categories, allowing statisticians to construct a representative basket and weights.
reference: 4.6 Price stability | 4.6.2 measurement of changes in the price level: consumer price index (CPI) and possible difficulties in measurement | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: Which item would have the greatest effect on the CPI if all items experienced the same percentage price rise?

options.label: A
options.text: The item with the smallest weight

options.label: B
options.text: The newest item in the basket

options.label: C
options.text: The item with the lowest initial price

options.label: D
options.text: The item with the largest weight

explanation: With the same percentage price change, the item carrying the greatest expenditure weight contributes the most to the weighted index.
reference: 4.6 Price stability | 4.6.2 measurement of changes in the price level: consumer price index (CPI) and possible difficulties in measurement | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: A CPI rises from 120 to 126. What is the inflation rate?
explanation: The inflation rate is the percentage change in the CPI: (126 - 120) / 120 × 100 = 5%.
reference: 4.6 Price stability | 4.6.2 measurement of changes in the price level: consumer price index (CPI) and possible difficulties in measurement | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A CPI falls from 150 to 147. What is the inflation rate?
explanation: The percentage change is (147 - 150) / 150 × 100 = -2%. The negative rate indicates deflation.
reference: 4.6 Price stability | 4.6.2 measurement of changes in the price level: consumer price index (CPI) and possible difficulties in measurement | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A CPI is 100 in the base year and 112 one year later. What does this show?

options.label: A
options.text: Every price rises 12%

options.label: B
options.text: The representative basket is 12% dearer

options.label: C
options.text: Households’ real incomes rise by 12% relative to the base year

options.label: D
options.text: Purchases of every basket item rise by exactly 12%

explanation: An index of 112 relative to a base of 100 means the weighted average cost of the representative basket is 12% higher than in the base year.
reference: 4.6 Price stability | 4.6.2 measurement of changes in the price level: consumer price index (CPI) and possible difficulties in measurement | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: What is a possible difficulty in using CPI to measure changes in the price level?

options.label: A
options.text: Average expenditure weights may poorly represent individual households.

options.label: B
options.text: Service prices cannot be included in a consumer basket.

options.label: C
options.text: Changing prices prevent calculation of a consumer price index.

options.label: D
options.text: Consumer prices directly measure the proportion of workers unemployed.

explanation: Different households have different expenditure patterns. A single representative basket may therefore overstate or understate the change in the cost of living for particular households.
reference: 4.6 Price stability | 4.6.2 measurement of changes in the price level: consumer price index (CPI) and possible difficulties in measurement | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: Why may changes in product quality create a CPI measurement problem?

options.label: A
options.text: Part of the higher price may pay for higher quality

options.label: B
options.text: Quality changes make all weights equal

options.label: C
options.text: Improved quality always lowers the nominal price

options.label: D
options.text: Quality changes prevent any price from being observed

explanation: If the quality of a product improves, part of its higher price may pay for a better product. Treating the entire price rise as inflation can overstate the rise in the cost of an equivalent standard of living.
reference: 4.6 Price stability | 4.6.2 measurement of changes in the price level: consumer price index (CPI) and possible difficulties in measurement | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: Why must the basket and weights used in a CPI be revised periodically?

options.label: A
options.text: The base year must always have an inflation rate of 100%

options.label: B
options.text: All products disappear from markets every year

options.label: C
options.text: Consumer spending patterns change over time

options.label: D
options.text: Revising weights guarantees that inflation is zero

explanation: New products appear, old products disappear and expenditure shares change. Updating the basket and weights helps the CPI remain representative.
reference: 4.6 Price stability | 4.6.2 measurement of changes in the price level: consumer price index (CPI) and possible difficulties in measurement | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: What is a nominal value?

options.label: A
options.text: A value at current prices

options.label: B
options.text: A value adjusted for inflation

options.label: C
options.text: A value expressed as a percentage of another quantity

options.label: D
options.text: A value measured only in physical units without reference to prices

explanation: Nominal, or money, values are measured in current prices. Real values adjust nominal values for changes in the price level.
reference: 4.6 Price stability | 4.6.3 distinction between money values (nominal) and real data | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: What is a real value?

options.label: A
options.text: A value measured only in cash

options.label: B
options.text: A value before any inflation adjustment

options.label: C
options.text: A value that must always be lower than its nominal value

options.label: D
options.text: A value adjusted for changes in the price level

explanation: Real data remove the effect of changes in the price level, allowing comparisons of purchasing power or output across time.
reference: 4.6 Price stability | 4.6.3 distinction between money values (nominal) and real data | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: Nominal wages rise by 4% while prices rise by 6%. What happens to real wages?

options.label: A
options.text: They rise

options.label: B
options.text: They are unchanged

options.label: C
options.text: They fall

options.label: D
options.text: They must double

explanation: Nominal wages rise more slowly than the price level, so the purchasing power of wages falls.
reference: 4.6 Price stability | 4.6.3 distinction between money values (nominal) and real data | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Nominal income rises by 8% while prices rise by 3%. What happens to real income?

options.label: A
options.text: It falls

options.label: B
options.text: It rises

options.label: C
options.text: It is unchanged

options.label: D
options.text: It becomes zero

explanation: Income rises faster than prices, so the purchasing power of the income increases.
reference: 4.6 Price stability | 4.6.3 distinction between money values (nominal) and real data | AO2 Analysis

prompt: What is demand-pull inflation?

options.label: A
options.text: Higher AD relative to AS

options.label: B
options.text: Inflation caused only by lower household spending

options.label: C
options.text: Inflation caused by lower production costs

options.label: D
options.text: Inflation caused by a fall in the price level

explanation: Demand-pull inflation occurs when aggregate demand increases and the economy cannot match the extra spending with an equivalent increase in aggregate supply.
reference: 4.6 Price stability | 4.6.4 causes of inflation: cost-push and demand-pull inflation | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: What is cost-push inflation?

options.label: A
options.text: Inflation driven by higher production costs

options.label: B
options.text: Inflation driven by lower AD

options.label: C
options.text: Inflation driven only by higher consumer confidence, with costs unchanged

options.label: D
options.text: Inflation driven by productivity gains

explanation: Cost-push inflation results when production costs rise and short-run aggregate supply decreases, pushing the general price level upward.
reference: 4.6 Price stability | 4.6.4 causes of inflation: cost-push and demand-pull inflation | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: Which change is most likely to cause demand-pull inflation?

options.label: A
options.text: A fall in consumer spending

options.label: B
options.text: A large rise in AD near full capacity

options.label: C
options.text: A rise in labour productivity

options.label: D
options.text: A fall in imported raw-material prices

explanation: A strong increase in aggregate demand creates greater upward pressure on prices when spare capacity is limited and output cannot expand easily.
reference: 4.6 Price stability | 4.6.4 causes of inflation: cost-push and demand-pull inflation | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: Which change is most likely to cause cost-push inflation?

options.label: A
options.text: Lower public spending

options.label: B
options.text: Falling foreign demand for the economy’s exports

options.label: C
options.text: More saving

options.label: D
options.text: Wage growth exceeding productivity growth

explanation: If wages rise faster than productivity, unit labour costs increase. Higher production costs can shift SRAS left and create cost-push inflation.
reference: 4.6 Price stability | 4.6.4 causes of inflation: cost-push and demand-pull inflation | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: A country's currency depreciates and imported raw materials become more expensive. What inflationary pressure may result?

options.label: A
options.text: Demand-pull inflation only

options.label: B
options.text: Cost-push inflation

options.label: C
options.text: Deflation

options.label: D
options.text: Disinflation by definition

explanation: More expensive imported inputs raise firms' production costs. This can shift SRAS left and create cost-push inflation.
reference: 4.6 Price stability | 4.6.4 causes of inflation: cost-push and demand-pull inflation | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Which is a likely consequence of unexpected inflation for a person whose money income is fixed?

options.label: A
options.text: A fall in purchasing power

options.label: B
options.text: A guaranteed rise in real income

options.label: C
options.text: A fall in every individual price

options.label: D
options.text: A guaranteed increase in the real value of savings

explanation: If money income is fixed while the general price level rises, the income buys fewer goods and services. Purchasing power therefore falls.
reference: 4.6 Price stability | 4.6.5 consequences of inflation | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: Why can inflation reduce a country's international competitiveness?

options.label: A
options.text: Domestic products become relatively more expensive

options.label: B
options.text: Labour productivity rises

options.label: C
options.text: The currency appreciates automatically in response to the rise in prices

options.label: D
options.text: Foreign-currency export prices fall

explanation: If domestic prices rise faster than those of trading partners, domestic products become relatively more expensive, which can reduce competitiveness.
reference: 4.6 Price stability | 4.6.5 consequences of inflation | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: Why may high and unstable inflation discourage investment?

options.label: A
options.text: Every future price becomes predictable

options.label: B
options.text: Real profits rise

options.label: C
options.text: Firms no longer need to plan for future production and investment

options.label: D
options.text: Future costs and returns become less certain

explanation: Unstable inflation makes future revenues, costs and real returns harder to predict. This uncertainty can make firms more reluctant to commit to long-term investment.
reference: 4.6 Price stability | 4.6.5 consequences of inflation | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: The CPI rises from 160 to 168 and then to 172.2. Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: The economy experiences deflation in the second period

options.label: B
options.text: The inflation rate is 8% in both periods

options.label: C
options.text: The price level falls in the second period

options.label: D
options.text: The economy experiences disinflation in the second period

explanation: The first inflation rate is 5%. The second is (172.2 - 168)/168 × 100 = 2.5%. Prices are still rising, but at a lower rate, so there is disinflation.

prompt:
The table shows the percentage price change and CPI weight for four categories. Which category contributes most to inflation?
| Category | Weight (%) | Price change (%) |
| food | 30 | 4 |

options.text: Food

options.label: B

options.label: C

options.label: D

prompt: A CPI basket has only two categories. Food has a weight of 60% and rises in price by 5%; transport has a weight of 40% and falls in price by 2%. What is the approximate CPI inflation rate?

prompt: The prices of half the items in a CPI basket rise and the prices of the other half fall. Why can the CPI still rise?

options.label: A
options.text: Falling prices are ignored

options.label: B
options.text: Each rising price enters the calculation twice

options.label: C
options.text: Weights and price changes vary

options.label: D
options.text: The index depends only on how many separate product prices rise

explanation: The CPI is a weighted average. A small number of heavily weighted or sharply rising items can outweigh more numerous price falls.
reference: 4.6 Price stability | 4.6.2 measurement of changes in the price level: consumer price index (CPI) and possible difficulties in measurement | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A household spends a much larger share of its income on rent than the representative CPI household. Rent rises faster than the overall CPI. What is most likely?

options.label: A
options.text: Its cost of living may rise faster than headline CPI

options.label: B
options.text: The household must experience deflation

options.label: C
options.text: The CPI must be mathematically incorrect

options.label: D
options.text: The household's nominal income must rise at the same rate as rent

explanation: A CPI reflects an average basket. A household with a larger-than-average weight on a rapidly rising item can experience a higher personal inflation rate.
reference: 4.6 Price stability | 4.6.2 measurement of changes in the price level: consumer price index (CPI) and possible difficulties in measurement | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Which change is most likely to make an existing CPI basket less representative?

options.label: A
options.text: The base year stays at 100

options.label: B
options.text: More spending on new products

options.label: C
options.text: Prices are collected from a range of different retail outlets

options.label: D
options.text: Weights reflect expenditure shares

explanation: If consumer preferences change and new products gain importance, a fixed basket based on older spending patterns becomes less representative.
reference: 4.6 Price stability | 4.6.2 measurement of changes in the price level: consumer price index (CPI) and possible difficulties in measurement | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: A new smartphone costs more than the old model but also has substantially better features. Why is this a measurement problem for CPI?

options.label: A
options.text: Improved features establish that the nominal price change is zero.

options.label: B
options.text: Quality improvements complicate identifying the pure price change.

options.label: C
options.text: Improved features establish that the measured inflation rate is negative.

options.label: D
options.text: Quality improvements establish that the whole price rise is inflation.

explanation: Quality improvements mean a like-for-like price comparison is difficult. Without adjustment, part of the price increase may be incorrectly treated as inflation.
reference: 4.6 Price stability | 4.6.2 measurement of changes in the price level: consumer price index (CPI) and possible difficulties in measurement | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: A CPI is based on a survey of 2 000 households. What is one reason its weights may still be inaccurate for the whole economy?

options.label: A
options.text: Only one household may be included

options.label: B
options.text: Sample spending patterns may differ from the population

options.label: C
options.text: Weights apply only to periods in which consumer prices are falling

options.label: D
options.text: Sampling changes wages

explanation: A household survey uses a sample. If the sample is unrepresentative or spending is reported inaccurately, estimated weights may differ from economy-wide patterns.
reference: 4.6 Price stability | 4.6.2 measurement of changes in the price level: consumer price index (CPI) and possible difficulties in measurement | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: Why can substitution by consumers cause a fixed-basket CPI to overstate the rise in the cost of living?

options.label: A
options.text: Consumers buy more of goods whose relative prices rise

options.label: B
options.text: Substitution lowers the base index below zero

options.label: C
options.text: Old weights omit shifts toward cheaper goods

options.label: D
options.text: Cheaper substitutes have zero weight

explanation: A fixed basket may assume consumers continue buying the same quantities even when relative prices change. In practice, substitution toward cheaper goods can reduce the actual increase in living costs.
reference: 4.6 Price stability | 4.6.2 measurement of changes in the price level: consumer price index (CPI) and possible difficulties in measurement | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: A worker's nominal wage rises from $30 000 to $32 400 while the CPI rises from 120 to 126. What happens to the worker's real wage?

options.label: A

prompt: Consumer confidence rises sharply when the economy has little spare capacity. Which sequence is most likely?

options.label: A
options.text: Consumption falls, SRAS shifts right and cost-push inflation increases

options.label: B

options.label: B
options.text: Economy X

options.label: C

options.label: D

explanation: As an economy approaches capacity, aggregate supply becomes less responsive. A given increase in AD therefore has a larger effect on the price level and a smaller effect on real output.

prompt: Most wages, pensions, tax thresholds and interest contracts are perfectly indexed to the CPI. Which consequence of anticipated inflation would be reduced most directly?

options.label: A
options.text: CPI measurement error

options.label: B
options.text: Arbitrary redistribution of purchasing power

options.label: C
options.text: Imported costs

options.label: D
options.text: The possibility of inflation caused by excessive aggregate demand

explanation: Indexation adjusts nominal contracts for inflation, reducing unplanned transfers between fixed-income recipients, borrowers, lenders and taxpayers. It does not eliminate the causes of inflation or measurement problems.

prompt: Inflation is 10% in country X and 15% in its main trading partners. All exchange rates are unchanged. Which statement is most accurate?

options.label: A
options.text: X may gain relative price competitiveness

options.label: B
options.text: X loses competitiveness

options.label: C
options.text: X experiences deflation relative to the prices measured in its base year

options.label: D
options.text: X’s real wages increase by exactly five percentage points

explanation: Competitiveness depends on relative price changes. If X's prices rise more slowly than its trading partners', its products can become relatively cheaper even though X has high inflation.
reference: 4.6 Price stability | 4.6.5 consequences of inflation | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Which statement best evaluates a fall in inflation from 12% to 4%?

options.label: A
options.text: It is deflation because inflation fell by 8 percentage points

options.label: B
options.text: The price level must fall back to its earlier level

options.label: C
options.text: Disinflation: prices still rise, but more slowly

options.label: D
options.text: It guarantees that every household's real income rises

explanation: The inflation rate is still positive, so prices continue to rise. Lower and more stable inflation can reduce uncertainty, but real-income effects still depend on changes in nominal incomes.

prompt: Which statement best summarises the usefulness and limitation of CPI as a measure of price stability?

options.label: A
options.text: It precisely measures the price change experienced by every household

options.label: B
options.text: A useful weighted average, but not each household's exact cost of living

options.label: C
options.text: It is useless because not every individual price moves in the same direction

options.label: D
options.text: It measures only producer costs and therefore cannot reflect consumer prices

explanation: CPI is valuable because it summarises a large set of prices using expenditure weights. Its limitation is that a representative basket cannot perfectly match the spending pattern or quality experience of every household.
reference: 4.6 Price stability | 4.6.2 measurement of changes in the price level: consumer price index (CPI) and possible difficulties in measurement | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: The CPI rises from 120 to 126 while a worker’s nominal wage and fixed nominal debt remain unchanged. Which pair of real changes follows?

options.label: A
options.text: Real wage rises; real debt burden rises.

options.label: B
options.text: Real wage falls; real debt burden falls.

options.label: C
options.text: Real wage rises; real debt burden falls.

options.label: D
options.text: Real wage falls; real debt burden rises.

explanation: A higher price level reduces the purchasing power of an unchanged money wage and the purchasing-power value of an unchanged nominal debt. Both fall by 1 − 120/126, approximately 4.76%.
